'''Georges Amsel''' (7 May 1933 – 11 March 2017) was a French [[physicist]], Director of Research at the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]].<ref>[https://www.ina.fr/video/I04089558 Georges Amsel est interrogé sur l'équipement nucléaire irakien]</ref>

==Biography==
Georges was born on 7 May 1933 in [[Budapest]], [[Hungary]] to Hugo and Sara (Fried) Amsel. After having been deported from Hungary in 1944, and finding refuge in [[Switzerland]]
in 1945, he undertook high-school studies in [[Geneva]] and then in [[Paris]], continuing
on in the [[Physics]] [[Laboratory]] of [[Ecole Normale Supérieure]] to obtain his [[doctorate]] in nuclear
physics in 1963.<ref name=hev /><ref name=bio>[https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/10420150.2012.655916 How it happened: 1959 to 2010 Georges Amsel, Ecole Normale Supérieure Paris, Groupe de Physique des Solides, Weizmann Institute, Israël, GPS Jussieu INSP Paris]</ref> During his doctoral study, and under the guidance of [[Pierre Aigrain]] he researched the possibilities for [[Particle detector|charged particle detection]] offered by [[Diode#Types of semiconductor diode|semiconductor diodes]] and developed some of the first such detectors in 1959.
He was invited to the first conference on semiconductor detectors, held at [[Asheville, North Carolina|Asheville]], [[North Carolina|NC]],
in 1960, where he presented the first [[Rutherford backscattering spectrometry]] to be obtained with a semiconductor detector.<ref name=bio /> During this period, he studied low-energy nuclear
reactions on stable [[isotopes]], developing [[anodization|anodizing]] methods for manufacturing
thin, self-supporting oxide films enriched in specific stable [[oxygen]] isotopes in collaboration
with [[David Samuel, 3rd Viscount Samuel|David Samuel]] at the [[Weizmann Institute]] in [[Israel]]. With these targets, he discovered the
narrow resonances in the <sup>18</sup>O(p,a)<sup>15</sup>N nuclear reaction. These discoveries were immediately put
to use in the field of stable isotopic tracing of atomic transport processes during thin-film growth
and transformation.<ref name=bio /> 
In 1968, he headed the installation of the HVEC AN2500 accelerator in the Solid State Physics 
group of the [[Ecole Normale Supérieure]]. it was one of the first nuclear particle accelerators to be installed in a condensed matter physics laboratory rather than in a nuclear physics laboratory. During this time,
he also laid down the foundations of the stochastic treatment of charged particle energy
loss processes, opening the way to rapid and accurate calculations of excitation curves obtained
around narrow nuclear resonances, and providing an approach to calculating
the overshoot on the leading edge, due to the Lewis effect. He has helped in setting up several [[Ion beam analysis|IBA]] [[laboratory|laboratories]] around the world and was the director of [[Accélérateur Grand Louvre d'analyse élémentaire|AGLAE, the accelerator at the Louvre museum]] dedicated to analysis of cultural heritage materials.<ref name=bio />

==Awards and honors==
* 1964, [[CNRS Bronze Medal]].<ref name=bio />
* 1971, [[CNRS Silver Medal]].<ref name=bio />
* 1984, [http://www.icaa-mtaa.org/ICAA%20wiki/Hevesy%20Medal%20Awards%20since%201968.aspx Hevesy Medal] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201008012732/http://www.icaa-mtaa.org/ICAA%20wiki/Hevesy%20Medal%20Awards%20since%201968.aspx |date=2020-10-08 }}.<ref name=hev>[https://akademiai.com/doi/abs/10.1007/BF02168023?journalCode=10967 1984 Hevesy Medal awarded to Georges Amsel]</ref>
* 1987, [[French Academy of Sciences|SERVANT prize of the French Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=bio />
* 1989, [[Ordre des Arts et des Lettres|Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters]].<ref name=bio />
* 1993, Félix Robin prize from the [[Société Française de Physique|French Physical Society]].<ref name=bio />
Member of [[Société Française de Physique]], [[Institute of Physics]].<ref name=bio />
